extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of comparative mythology; readers interested in folklore and myth classification
extracted.subtask_description: A typology and descriptive classification of major myth-classes (creation, flood, hero, fire, star, death, taboo, dismemberment, dualism, etc.) with cross-cultural examples and comparative tables to indicate geographical incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation myths (creation of the earth and man)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation myths (creation of the earth and man).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually involve a vast world of waters from which the creative agency raises the earth, by word, will-power, or physical labour. Examples cited: Babylonians (Merodach forms heaven and earth), Persians (Ormuzd), Greeks (Uranus and Gæa), Teutons (world from body of Ymir), Hindus (Brahma/boar), Japanese (Izanagi and Izanami), many American and Oceanic examples. See chapter on cosmogony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths of the origin of man
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths of the origin of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely allied to creation myths; man is often made from clay or the dust of the earth, sometimes moistened with divine blood/sweat and given the breath of life. Some myths feature prior wooden men or evolution from animals/caves. Examples include Prometheus (Greeks), Brahma (Hindus), various American and Oceanic traditions (coyotes, apes, turtle, maize).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flood myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Flood myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account of a great deluge drowning living things except a favored individual or family. Cross-cultural examples listed: Egyptians, Babylonians (Ut-Napishtim), Hebrews (Noah), Persians (Yima), Greeks (Deucalion), Hindus (Manu), and many American tribes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths of a place of reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths of a place of reward (the celestial garden of God).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification of cultural equivalents of paradisiacal realms (e.g., Egyptians: Aalu; Persians: Alburz; Greeks: Elysian Fields; Romans: Fortunate Isles; Celts: the Otherworld beyond/beneath the sea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths of a place of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths of a place of punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paired with reward-myths; traditions have concepts of places of punishment or underworld realms (treatment varies by culture; examples discussed elsewhere in the volume).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sun myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Sun myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sun-centred myths already treated elsewhere in the volume; often connected with creator and life-giving roles and with cosmological cycles (examples appear throughout comparative tables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moon myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Moon myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previously treated in the volume; often associated with cycles, regeneration, or death/resurrection themes (e.g., moon as bringer or messenger regarding mortality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Hero myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture-hero or hero myths treated individually; include origin and adventures of exceptional figures who civilize or protect peoples (see separate chapter). Examples: Perseus, Heracles, Sargon, Moses, Romulus, Rama, Uitzilopochtli, Hun-Apu and Xbalanque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beast myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Beast myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beasts and birds credited with divine or semi-divine attributes; many cultures have animal deities or sacred beasts (examples: Greek Io as a cow, Ahts thunder-bird, Banks Islanders' Marawa the spider, various Native American examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths to account for customs or rites
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths to account for customs or rites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Etiological tales explaining origins or reasons for cultural customs and rituals; often provide 'just-so' explanations linking ritual practice to myth history (many examples across Europe and indigenous cultures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths of journeys or adventures through the Underworld/place of the dead
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths of journeys or adventures through the Underworld or place of the dead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives describing descent, travel, or return from the Otherworld; include ferrying of souls (Charon), epic underworld journeys of heroes, and culturally specific afterlife topographies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths regarding the birth of gods
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths regarding the birth of gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts of divine births—often miraculous or involving virgin birth motifs; comparative examples include Greek, Vedic, Algonquin, Huron, Mexican, Peruvian, Thlinkeet, and Uapès traditions (detailed lists in comparative tables).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two major descriptions: (1) myths of destruction of the world by fire (universal conflagration), and (2) myths of fire being stolen from heaven and brought to mankind (fire-stealing). Destruction-by-fire examples are numerous in the Americas (Arawaks, Aztecs, Algonquins, Peruvians) and present in Old World eschatologies (Jewish last day, Norse Ragnarök, Roman ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire-stealing myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire-stealing myths (a subclass of fire myths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories in which a demigod, hero, or supernatural bird steals fire from Heaven to benefit humankind (e.g., Prometheus bringing fire in a hollow cane; widespread cross-cultural parallels with birds or trickster figures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Star myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Star myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myths dealing with constellations and star-groups rather than single stars; often link stars to ancestors, objects, or events. Constellations like Orion, the Pleiades, Great Bear, Cross, and the Milky Way have universal or regionally recurrent interpretations (examples and rich South American material provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths of death
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths of death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ætiological narratives manufactured to account for death—often explained as consequence of breaking a taboo, neglecting ritual, or magic. Examples include Pandora/Greek apple, Polynesian, Southern Indian, Central African and many indigenous explanations; comparative examples listed in tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food of the dead formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Food of the dead formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ritual or mythic motifs concerning provisions for the dead (formulaic motifs appearing in burial/afterlife beliefs); listed among myth-classes though specific examples are treated in the volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths regarding taboo
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths regarding taboo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that explain the existence, origin, and necessity for taboos or forbidden things (e.g., Cupid and Psyche, name-taboo stories like Lohengrin, Adam and Eve). Often linked to social regulation—examples from Greeks, Teutons, Australians, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Dismemberment' myths
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Dismemberment' myths (in which a god is dismembered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myths where a god or demigod is torn to pieces and parts scattered and reassembled (e.g., Osiris, Dionysus, Demeter analogues). Often interpreted as originating from burial of a human victim in crops and symbolic of resurrection; practiced or commemorated in ritual contexts; many cross-cultural instances listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dualistic myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Dualistic myths (the good god fighting the bad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief in opposing good and evil deities, found both among advanced theological systems (e.g., Persian Ormuzd and Ahriman) and among traditions influenced by outsiders. Examples include many pairs across cultures (Zeus/Typhon, Apollo/Python, Thor/Loki, Indra/Ahi, numerous native pairs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths of the origin of the arts of life (culture myths)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture myths: myths of the origin of the arts of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tales in which a god or culture-hero teaches humans useful arts and civilizing knowledge (e.g., Osiris, Oannes, Prometheus, Bacchus, Cadmus, Nuada, Wieland the Smith, Okikurimi, many indigenous culture-heroes listed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Soul myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Soul myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myths treating separation, concealment, or journey of a person's life, heart, or soul (life-tokens/life-index), and passage to the Otherworld; include examples worldwide (Egyptian two brothers, Samson and Delilah, Meleager, Styx/Charon motifs, life-locks among Eskimos, birth-trees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative tables of myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative tables of myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compiled to bring together the most important types of myth and indicate their geographical incidence; intended as a ready reference to parallels (not exhaustive but carefully compiled). The chapter supplies extensive cross-cultural lists and examples for each myth-type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of vegetation/plant-spirits in festival practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropomorphic representations of tree- or plant-spirits in folk festivals (e.g., 'Burry Man', 'Jack-in-the-Green', 'Little May Rose').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Folkloric criterion: many spring/vegetation festivals personify vegetation as leaf- or tree-clad figures (examples from South Queensferry, Bohemia, Alsace, Lithuania, Brie, Frankenwald, Thuringia, Carinthia, England). These traditions are evidence for the survival of ancient vegetation-spirit cults and link ritual practice to mythic regeneration themes.
